However, it is limited to single light sources and lacks full volumetric depth information, leading to artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts [S3, book][S4, unofficial].

The claim states that the technique is limited to single light sources, lacks full volumetric depth information, and leads to artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts. Source [S3] explicitly states: 'Light shafts from background objects can appear in front of foreground objects when dealing with relatively near light sources, because the method lacks full volumetric depth information.' It also notes that the technique is applied to 'one or more image light sources' but the implementation described (and the specific artifact issue) relates to the screen-space limitation where occlusion is estimated per-pixel without true depth, leading to the described artifacts. Source [S4] confirms the limitation to 'a single, visible light source' and describes the screen-space nature which lacks true volumetric data. Therefore, all parts of the claim are supported by the provided evidence.

It builds on [Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching)](3873-volumetric-light-shafts-urp-raymarching.md) by simplifying the volume rendering equation to estimate single in-scattering from a single light source, modulated by an estimated occlusion factor derived from radial sampling [S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the method builds on Volumetric Light Shafts by simplifying the volume rendering equation to estimate single in-scattering from a single light source, modulated by an estimated occlusion factor derived from radial sampling. Source [S5] explicitly confirms these points: it mentions simplifying the VRE to approximate in-scattering from the sun (single light source), assumes single scattering only, and estimates occlusion D(phi) by sampling along a ray to the light source in image space (radial sampling). All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported

*   The accumulation approximates the integral of in-scattered light, where the decay simulates absorption/scattering over distance [S3, book][S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the accumulation approximates the integral of in-scattered light and that decay simulates absorption/scattering over distance. Source [S3] explicitly describes the algorithm as a summation (accumulation) of samples where 'decayi... dissipates each sample's contribution as the ray progresses away from the light source' and models attenuation. Source [S5] confirms that the method approximates 'in-scattering from the sun' and uses 'decay' to control the summation, noting that the underlying physics involves extinction (absorption/scattering) coefficients. Both sources support the interpretation that the decay factor simulates the loss of light (absorption/scattering) over the distance sampled.
